title: Golden Horde
summary: After the Mongol armies returned from central Europe, Batu set up the Golden Horde, also called the Khanate of Qipchaq, in the 1240s, with its capital at Sarai on the lower Volga. Its khans ruled a multiethnic realm reaching into western Siberia and took tribute from the Russian princes, later backing Moscow. The Horde split into separate khanates in the 1400s, Ivan III stopped paying tribute, and the Crimean Tatars dealt the final blow in 1502.

uncertainty.note: Dating start to c. 1242 when Batu withdrew from Central Europe and organized Sarai as his permanent seat in the 1240s; Jochi received the western appanage in 1227. End is dated to 1502 when the Crimean Khanate sacked Sarai, though Russian tribute formally lapsed after the Ugra standoff in 1480.

as_recorded.value: 1240s after the return of the Mongol force that invaded central Europe

where.modern_name: Selitrennoye archaeological site, Astrakhan Oblast, Russia (identified with Sarai, capital of the Golden Horde)

importance.justification: Held the Russian principalities as tributaries for over two centuries and shaped the rise of Moscow (R3 D3 T3 L3).

related.because: The Golden Horde originated as the western appanage (Ulus of Jochi) granted to Genghis Khan's eldest son.
Batu Khan established his permanent capital at Sarai on the lower Volga following his western campaigns across Russia and Central Europe.
Papal envoy Giovanni da Pian del Carpine stopped at Batu's camp on the lower Volga on his journey to the Mongol capital Karakorum.
The Golden Horde subjected the former principalities of Kievan Rus to periodic census and heavy taxation, fundamentally reorganizing East Slavic political power.
